For the English translations of Adams’s French original, I have relied on Michael Adams, “Some Account of a Journey to the Frozen Sea, and of the Discovery of the Carcase of a Mammoth,” The New York Medical and Philosophical Journal and Review, vol. 2 (2) (1810), pp. 141-153. Quotation on p. 142. Elsewhere in work-in-progress, I discuss the translation from French to English and the role of Adams’s account in establishing tropes surrounding the nature of refrigeration in the nineteenth century. This roundabout history of translation likely speaks tot he limited availability of the Journal du Nord in western Europe. Georges Cuvier and Bernard, Comte de Lacepede, “Rapport à la classe des sciences physiques et mathématiques de l’Institut [sur le cadavre, d’un animal découvert dans la Mer Glaciale, et intitulé Mammouth,” Annales du Muséum d’Histoire Naturelle [Paris] 10 (1807), pp. 381-86. Despite the indirect route to publication Cuvier and Lacépède held that because of “the import of the object, and because ambiguous expressions had already given a place to several errors in publication or in conversation, we do not believe it useless to put in text several observations.” (p. 381).

In an addendum to the first volume of Récherches sur les ossemens fossiles, Cuvier wrote that the hair of the mammoth “proves, without a doubt, that these fossil elephants were animals of a cold country, and that they did not inhabit the torrid zone.” Georges Cuvier, “Additions et Corrections à faire aux tomes II, III, et IV de cet ouvrage,” in Récherches sur les ossemens fossiles de quadrupèdes: où l’on rétablit les caractères de olusiers espèces d’animaux que les révoltions du globe paraissent avoir détruites, 1st edition, vol. 1 (Paris: Chez Deterville, 1812), 13. And in more extended form in scientific and quasi-scientific genres. Bassett Digby provides an embellished account in The Mammoth and Mammoth-Hunting, in which Adams, an adjunct of the St Petersburg Academy of Science, is promoted to professor, and Schoumacoff becomes “Schumarov,” an even more hapless character than in the Adams original reliant upon “Dutch courage—a vodka bottle in each pocket” (104) to overcome his cultural superstitions attached to the mammoth. Digby, Mammoth and Mammoth-Hunting, pp, 103-107. Digby himself went to Yakutsk in the early 1920s, so it is possible that his emendations were based on new first-hand knowledge, although cultural chauvinism and contemporary racism are more likely explanations.
